objective: Help de-escalate an angry or agitated client, and stay with or near the client after an emergency medication to monitor its effect
secondaryObjectives: Recognizing the potential for violence and using safety precautions

sources.cite: 2026 PN licensure test plan: Psychosocial Integrity (12%)
sources.note: Relayed from the course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/nursing.ts), which read it 2026-09-18; the objective title is the course's own.

sources.cite: Richmond JS, Berlin JS, Fishkind AB, et al. Verbal de-escalation of the agitated patient: consensus statement of the American Association for Emergency Psychiatry Project BETA De-escalation Workgroup. West J Emerg Med 2012;13(1):17-25. Ten domains of verbal de-escalation; restraint 'always as a last resort'
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes). Domains: respect personal space (two arm's lengths); do not be provocative; one person establishes verbal contact; be concise; identify wants and feelings; listen closely; agree or agree to disagree; set clear limits; offer choices and optimism; debrief the patient and staff. The paper names delirium, psychosis and intoxication among the causes of a patient's inability to conform.

sources.cite: Abderhalden C, Needham I, Dassen T, et al. Predicting inpatient violence using an extended version of the Broset-Violence-Checklist. BMC Psychiatry 2006;6:17. The checklist's six behaviors: confused, irritable, boisterous, verbally threatening, physically threatening, attacking objects (each present or absent); a total over 2 was the original cut-off
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch). The study predicted attacks during the next shift; the sim uses the checklist only to name the behaviors a nurse scores.

sources.cite: 42 CFR 482.13(e): restraint only when less restrictive interventions have been ineffective, on an order, for the shortest time; for violent or self-destructive behavior, a face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour and an order of no more than 4 hours for an adult

brief.situation: Tyler Grant, 29 (a fictional client), was admitted to an inpatient mental health unit two days ago in a manic episode. He has slept two hours a night. At 20:15 another client moved his notebook, and Tyler is now pacing the day room, shouting, 'Touch my stuff again and see what happens. I'll make him sorry.' Three other clients are watching. You are a licensed practical nurse on the unit; the RN is in the medication room and there is an as-needed emergency medication order for agitation. You have about 30 minutes.
handover: Manic episode, day 2; little sleep; no violence so far on the unit.

Unit policy: de-escalate first; the RN decides on and gives an emergency medication; after it, a nurse stays with or near the client and checks vital signs, sedation and breathing every 15 minutes for the first hour; restraint only on a time-limited order after less restrictive measures fail.
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Tyler reacts at once; then let the situation continue, which moves the clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His trust and distress change with what you do. Space, one calm voice and choices bring him down.
Your time ends at 30 minutes. Afterward you write a short summary, then document what you found and what you did.

source.note: About 30 minutes in the evening on an inpatient mental health unit (author's scenario timing).
How trust and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a patient.

checkIn.label: Alone and calm, two arm's lengths away: 'Tyler, it's the nurse. I can see you're upset. I'm listening.'

effects.log: You approach alone, stop two arm's lengths away at an angle, hands open, and speak calmly.

effects.finding: "He went through my notebook! My whole plan's in there!"

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: He stops for a second. "Yes! Finally someone gets it."

normalize.label: Set a limit and offer a choice: 'I need you to stop shouting. Quiet room or your own room?'

effects.log: You set one clear limit and offer him a choice.

screen.label: Ask him directly whether he means to hurt someone, or himself
screen.why: He has answered; go on to the follow-up questions.

effects.log: You ask him directly whether he means to hurt the other client, or himself.

then.finding: "No. I just want my stuff left alone." No thoughts of hurting himself.

then.log: No intent toward anyone once asked; no thoughts of self-harm.

then.finding: "Just keep him away from me!" (Not calm enough to answer yet.)

scoreBvc.label: Note the Broset Violence Checklist behaviors for the RN

effects.log: You note which of the checklist's six behaviors you see.

effects.finding: Irritable, boisterous, verbally threatening, physically threatening (fists, stepping toward the other client): 4 of 6.

askWants.label: Ask what he wants right now

effects.log: You ask what he wants right now.

effects.finding: "My notebook back. And for people to stop touching my things."

askSleep.label: Ask how he has been sleeping and feeling
askSleep.available: not talking and (siKnown and not sleepAsked)
askSleep.why: Screen first (or you have asked this).

effects.log: You ask how he has been sleeping and how he feels in his body.

effects.finding: "Sleep's for later. My head's going a hundred miles an hour."

space.label: Move the other clients out of the day room and keep one calm voice

effects.log: You ask a nursing assistant to take the other clients to the TV room, and you stay the only one talking to Tyler.

effects.finding: With no audience, he slows his pacing.

notebook.label: Offer to get his notebook back for him
notebook.available: not talking and (wantsAsked and not notebookBack)
notebook.why: Ask what he wants first (or done).

effects.log: You offer to get his notebook from the other client.

effects.finding: The nursing assistant brings it. He clutches it. "Thank you."

tellRn.label: Report to the RN: threats, the checklist behaviors, what helped

effects.log: Keeping him in view, you call the RN over and report the threats, the checklist behaviors and what has helped.

effects.finding: The RN offers him the ordered emergency medication by mouth; he accepts it and takes it with water.

monitor.label: Stay near him and check vital signs, sedation and breathing every 15 minutes
monitor.available: not talking and (reported and not monitoring)
monitor.why: Report to the RN first (or done).

effects.log: You stay near him in the quiet room and check his vital signs, sedation level and breathing every 15 minutes.

effects.finding: At 15 minutes: pulse 88, breathing 16 and even, drowsy but easy to wake, no stiffness or muscle spasms. You report it to the RN.

crowd.label: Gather four staff around him to make him comply

effects.log: You gather four staff in a circle around him.

effects.finding: He backs into the corner, shouting louder.

effects.log: A show of force corners an agitated client and invites violence.

leaveAfter.label: Once he is calm, leave him to sleep it off

effects.log: Once he is calm, you leave him in the quiet room alone.

effects.finding: Nobody checks his breathing or sedation for the next hour.

effects.log: After an emergency medication a nurse stays with or near the client and monitors its effect.

reassure.why: Let the conversation continue first (the button above the actions).

formulation.question: Write your summary for the RN: what happened, the risk, and what you did before and after the medication.

parts.label: What happened and the risk
parts.criteria: Names a manic client with little sleep, triggered by another client moving his notebook; 4 of 6 checklist behaviors (high risk); no intent toward anyone once calmer; no self-harm thoughts.
parts.modelAnswer: In a manic episode with two hours of sleep a night, he was set off when another client moved his notebook: irritable, boisterous, threatening and stepping toward the other client, 4 of 6 on the checklist. Once calmer he said he did not mean to hurt anyone and had no thoughts of self-harm.

parts.label: What was done
parts.criteria: Names one calm voice at a distance, the others moved, a limit and a choice, his notebook returned, the RN told, the medication taken by mouth, and staying near with checks every 15 minutes.
parts.modelAnswer: One calm voice at two arm's lengths; the other clients moved out; a limit and a choice of rooms; his notebook returned; the RN told and the medication accepted by mouth; I stayed near and checked vital signs, sedation and breathing every 15 minutes, reporting each to the RN.

safe.headline: Good: calm, medicated and watched
safe.body: You led with space and one voice, explored the threat, answered what set him off, reported to the RN and stayed near to watch the medication's effect.

walkout.headline: It escalated
walkout.body: 'Calm down' and threats of seclusion push an agitated client further. One calm voice, a limit and a choice bring him down.

time_up.headline: Time up

scoring.modelReasoning: Within the practical nurse's role: approach alone and calm, keep distance, remove the audience, set one limit and offer choices, find and meet what set him off, ask directly about the threat and report to the RN. After the RN's emergency medication, stay with or near him and check vital signs, sedation and breathing so a reaction is caught early.
